title: Samuel Johnson's Letter to Lord Chesterfield
text:
In 1747 Samuel Johnson, a poor and little known London writer, published the plan for a great Dictionary of the English Language and addressed it to the Earl of Chesterfield, a famous man of taste who might act as his patron. Chesterfield gave him ten pounds and little else. Johnson later said he had waited in the earl's outer rooms and been turned away from his door.

For the next seven years Johnson worked on the dictionary almost alone, with a few hired copyists, in poverty. In late 1754, when the dictionary was about to appear, Chesterfield published two essays in a magazine praising the coming work and recommending Johnson as its author, apparently hoping to receive the dedication.

On February 7, 1755, Johnson wrote him a letter. He reminded him of the seven years he had waited and worked without one act of assistance. "Is not a Patron, my Lord," he asked, "one who looks with unconcern on a man struggling for life in the water, and when he has reached ground encumbers him with help?" The notice the earl had now chosen to take, he wrote, had come too late for him to enjoy it.

The Dictionary appeared that April, with no dedication. Boswell later published the letter in his Life of Johnson.
lesson: Support is worth most when it is needed, not after someone has succeeded without you. Offer help at the start, or do not expect gratitude at the end.
people: Samuel Johnson, Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
source: Samuel Johnson, letter to the Earl of Chesterfield, February 7, 1755, in James Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson (1791)
